No partial-gravity fire data in PSI yet

No PSI combustion investigation has burned anything at lunar (0.16 g) or Martian (0.38 g) gravity. NASA expects such data from the Lunar-g Combustion Investigation (LUCI) and Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2).
LUCI: simulated lunar gravity on a sounding rocket

LUCI burned a cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL) fabric and a 4 mm acrylic (PMMA) rod in air at normal pressure while the Blue Origin New Shepard capsule spun at about 11 rpm to imitate lunar gravity: the first extended (over 25 s) burns in simulated lunar gravity. The acrylic flame tip spread at about 1.5 mm/s. Results are in NASA presentations, not in PSI.
FM2: the first fire experiment on the Moon

FM2 will burn four samples, one at a time, in atmospheres planned for lunar habitats, with cameras and temperature, O₂ and CO₂ sensors. Drop-tower centrifuge tests behind it found that some materials burn at lower oxygen levels in lunar gravity than on Earth: less heat loss than at 1 g, yet enough buoyant flow to feed the flame.
NASA FM2 page; Zayac et al., NTRS 20240015307 (2024)
Mimicked partial gravity: ACME E-FIELD Flames (PSI-22)

A field of up to 10 kV between the burner and a mesh above it pushes on the ions a flame makes (chemi-ionization), driving ion-driven convection that stands in for buoyancy; microgravity lets this be studied without real buoyancy. That makes E-FIELD Flames the closest PSI comes to partial gravity. Its per-test data are not in the tables loaded here.
Bounding with 0 g and 1 g, and its limit

Microgravity and Earth results can bracket intermediate gravity: where a material behaves the same at both, that is the best available guess for the Moon. But the FM2 work shows the bracket is not always safe, since some materials are most flammable at lunar gravity. Materials whose 0 g and 1 g results disagree should be tested first.
